title: Ulyana and the Witness
premise: Tamsin Coldharbour, concierge at the Grand Meridian Hotel, built a quiet career on solving guests' small mysteries while remaining unseen themselves. When a letter arrives confessing to the murder of local judge Edmund Voss—a case closed three years ago when a drifter died awaiting trial—Tamsin realizes the confession is postmarked the day after Voss's funeral, written by someone who knew the hotel intimately. Following the letter's clues through the hotel's forgotten rooms and the town's buried loyalties, Tamsin discovers the real killer was protected by a conspiracy of respectable citizens who framed the drifter, and that the confessor is dying and wants justice before silence takes them. In the end, Tamsin must choose between exposing the truth through channels that failed once before, or orchestrating justice outside the law—forcing the guilty to confess publicly before the statute-bound trial of an accomplice begins.
about_author: Emrys Amberdale is the pen name of a former night-shift hotel worker who spent a decade collecting the secrets strangers leave behind in lobbies and elevators. They write mysteries about people who watch for a living, believing every building keeps better records than any police file.

chapters.title: The Day After
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Three years after Judge Voss's murder was 'solved,' Tamsin sorts the dead man's memorial mail at the Grand Meridian and finds a handwritten confession postmarked the day after his funeral. The emotional beat: dread wrapped in professional curiosity—the letter names the hotel, and Tamsin recognizes the handwriting style of someone trained here.

chapters.title: Invisible by Design
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, with flashback. We learn how Tamsin became the concierge who notices everything—raised in the hotel's back corridors by a housekeeper mother, taught that survival means being unremarkable. The beat: establishing why exposure terrifies them more than danger does.

chapters.title: What the Letter Knew
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Forensic reading of the confession reveals details never made public: the position of the body, a missing decanter, a second set of footprints. Only staff or police could know. The beat: the mystery tightens from 'who wrote this' to 'who was there.'

chapters.title: The Drifter's Grave
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin visits Callum Reeve's pauper's grave—the drifter convicted in the court of public opinion who died before trial. A woman in mourning black watches from the churchyard gate. The beat: guilt as a place you can stand in; Tamsin feels the town's complicity pressing down.

chapters.title: Room 412
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The confession's paper stock matches hotel stationery discontinued after Voss's death—and Room 412, sealed since the murder, still holds its original furnishings. Tamsin picks the lock. The beat: transgression and thrill; inside, they find scratch marks under the desk and a hidden key.

chapters.title: The Mourning Woman
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Tamsin and Ivy Sarn, the woman from the churchyard—Voss's former clerk. Ivy admits she received a copy of the same confession and has been too frightened to act. The beat: reluctant alliance; two watchers deciding, for once, to be seen together.

chapters.title: Staff Who Stayed
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Interviews with longtime employees reveal who had access in 412 the night Voss died: the night manager Dorian Pell, housekeeper Marga, and a bellhop who left town abruptly. Each alibi is polished—but polished things get noticed by people like Tamsin. The beat: suspicion spreading like damp through walls.

chapters.title: A Warning in the Laundry
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin finds their own locker emptied and a note: 'Closed cases stay closed.' Someone inside knows what they're doing. The beat: fear arrives personally; invisibility is being stripped away deliberately.

chapters.title: Marga's Hands
chapters.summary: Marga's POV. The elderly housekeeper remembers scrubbing something out of Room 412 the morning after the murder—on orders, for extra pay. She's kept silent for three years because her son works for Pell. The beat: complicity of the small and scared; memory as both wound and weapon.

chapters.title: The Confessor's Voice
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Handwriting analysis points to the vanished bellhop, Teodor Lasko. Tamsin traces him to a hospice two towns over—he's dying of the same illness that killed his sister, a former maid at the Meridian. The beat: the confessor found, but time running out on both justice and the witness.

chapters.title: What Teodor Saw
chapters.summary: Teodor's POV. From his hospice bed, Teodor recounts the night: he saw Pell and an unnamed 'gentleman' leave 412, saw them plant evidence against Callum Reeve, and stayed silent out of terror—until dying made silence unbearable. The beat: grief and relief entangled; the truth finally spoken aloud.

chapters.title: The Gentleman's Ring
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Teodor describes a signet ring; Tamsin matches it to Aldous Wrenn, the magistrate who closed the case and is now presiding over a related corruption trial beginning in ten days. The beat: the conspiracy reaches into the courthouse itself—justice outside the law may be the only kind available.

chapters.title: Pell Closes Ranks
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Dorian Pell confronts Tamsin with veiled threats and an offer: a promotion, a raise, forgetfulness. He mentions Tamsin's mother's old debts. The beat: temptation and insult braided together; Tamsin refuses, and understands they've crossed a line they can't uncross.

chapters.title: Ivy's Doubt
chapters.summary: Ivy's POV. Ivy wavers—Wrenn once saved her career, and going public could destroy her. She nearly burns her copy of the confession. The beat: the cost of conscience; loyalty to a flawed benefactor versus loyalty to a dead innocent man.

chapters.title: The Sealed Floor
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Using the key from 412, Tamsin opens the hotel's sealed archive floor and finds Voss's own private files: the judge was investigating Wrenn and Pell when he died. The beat: revelation recontextualizes everything—Voss wasn't a victim of random violence but of the investigation he was running.

chapters.title: They Know Your Name
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin is followed home, their apartment searched, the confession stolen. Pell makes it explicit: cooperate or be framed exactly as Callum Reeve was. The beat: darkest hour; the watcher becomes the watched, and Tamsin's lifelong strategy of invisibility fails completely.

chapters.title: Choosing to Be Seen
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, with Ivy present. Out of options inside the law—Wrenn controls the courts—Tamsin proposes the unthinkable: use the hotel itself as the instrument of justice, staging a gathering where the guilty will be forced to perform their innocence in front of witnesses who now know the truth. The beat: resolve forged from ruin; belonging chosen over safety.

chapters.title: The Grand Meridian Gala
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converging. On the anniversary gala, Tamsin engineers a sequence: Marga testifies to Ivy, Teodor's recorded voice plays through the ballroom speakers, and the stolen confession resurfaces—Tamsin anticipated the theft and copied it. The beat: controlled chaos; the hunters realize the trap was the hotel all along.

chapters.title: Confession Under Chandeliers
chapters.summary: Climax, Tamsin's POV. Cornered before forty witnesses and a journalist Ivy secretly invited, Pell breaks and implicates Wrenn, whose ring and signature close the chain of evidence. Wrenn attempts to flee through the service corridors—Tamsin's territory—and is stopped by staff who choose, one by one, to stand with Tamsin. The beat: triumph earned collectively; invisibility transformed into presence.

chapters.title: Aftermath of Light
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Wrenn and Pell are arrested; the case against Callum Reeve is formally vacated. Teodor dies peacefully days later, having heard the news. The beat: bittersweet victory; justice arrived late and imperfectly, but it arrived, and it took a whole community to carry it.

chapters.title: The Empty Chair
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. At Callum Reeve's belated memorial, the town that condemned him shows up awkwardly, apologetically. Ivy offers Tamsin a role as investigator-consultant; Tamsin hesitates, then accepts—not invisibility anymore, but chosen visibility. The beat: belonging achieved, not granted.

chapters.title: Concierge, Still
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Tamsin's POV. Back at the front desk, Tamsin helps a nervous guest find a lost letter of their own—a small mystery, gladly taken. In the drawer below, the original confession rests beside a new card: 'Cases accepted.' The beat: quiet closure; the watcher has become the keeper, and the door stays open for the next truth that checks in.
